title: 4D nucleome landscape reveals dissolution of bipartite active X chromosome in liver cancer development
abstract:
Nature Cell Biology, Published online: 11 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41556-026-02063-y

Xie, Tan, Mo and colleagues show that a liver-specific bipartite structure of the active X chromosome is lost early in hepatocarcinogenesis in mice and humans, driving X-linked gene activation and premalignant transformation, particularly in males.
headline: Cancer cells disable a protective structure in the X chromosome, fueling liver tumor growth.
why_it_matters: This discovery reveals an early warning sign of liver cancer development, especially in men who have only one X chromosome. Understanding this mechanism could lead to new ways to detect cancer early or block its progression before tumors form.
key_findings: The active X chromosome (the copy of the X chromosome that cells use) normally has a special two-part structure in liver cells that keeps genes organized and controlled.
This protective structure breaks down early in liver cancer development, both in mouse models and human patients.
When the structure dissolves, X-linked genes (genes located on the X chromosome) become abnormally active, causing cells to transform into a precancerous state.
Men appear especially vulnerable because they have only one X chromosome, so losing this protection has a bigger impact on their cells.
The findings suggest this structural collapse is a driver of cancer, not just a side effect—meaning it actually helps cancer get started.
methods_snapshot: Researchers used 4D imaging and mapping techniques (methods that track chromosome structure and gene activity over time) to watch how the X chromosome's architecture changes in normal liver cells versus cancer cells. They studied this in both laboratory mice and human tissue samples to confirm their findings.

glossary.definition: One of two sex chromosomes; females have two copies, males have one.
The working copy of the X chromosome that a cell uses to make proteins; the other copy is usually inactive.
A two-part organized arrangement that helps control how genes are packaged and used in cells.
Genes located on the X chromosome that can be inherited differently in males and females.
The process of normal liver cells gradually turning into liver cancer cells.
The early step when a normal cell begins to show cancer-like behavior but hasn't become a full tumor yet.
A map of how chromosomes inside the cell nucleus are arranged and interact over time (the '4D' means three dimensions of space plus time).

limitations: The study was primarily conducted in mouse models, so the findings need confirmation in more human patients to fully understand how this mechanism works in real-world liver cancer. It remains unclear whether this X chromosome change happens in all liver cancers or only in certain subtypes.
